lead: A wing box with a middle spar, or a fuselage with a floor, has two or more closed cells. Under torque each cell carries its own constant shear flow, the wall between two cells carries the difference, and every cell must twist at the same rate because they are joined. The torque equation plus one equal-twist equation per extra cell gives the flows. The same equations, with the open-section flow added, solve the cells under shear and locate the shear centre.
prereq: You need: Bredt–Batho torsion and the twist-rate integral from the previous chapter, and the cut-and-add method of the closed-section shear chapter.

blocks.text: A single cell has one unknown flow, fixed by T = 2Aq. Two cells have two: q₁ circulating round cell 1 and q₂ round cell 2, both taken anticlockwise. The outer walls of cell 1 carry q₁ and those of cell 2 carry q₂. On the shared wall the two circulations run in opposite directions, so it carries q₁ − q₂ in the sense of cell 1.

blocks.where: T is the torque (N·mm); A₁ and A₂ are the areas enclosed by cells 1 and 2 (mm²); q₁ and q₂ are the cell flows (N/mm).
dθ/dz is the rate of twist of cell R (rad/mm); the integral goes round cell R only, using the net flow in each wall, q₁ − q₂ in the shared wall; G is the shear modulus (N/mm²).

blocks.text: Because the cells are joined along their common wall and the ribs keep the section shape, every cell has the same rate of twist. That equal-twist condition is the second equation, and the one most often left out.

Write δ for ∮ds/t taken over a group of walls (dimensionless): δ₁ round all of cell 1, δ₂ round all of cell 2, and δ₁₂ for the shared wall alone. Then ∮₁q ds/t = δ₁q₁ − δ₁₂q₂ and ∮₂q ds/t = δ₂q₂ − δ₁₂q₁.

items: Number the cells and take every cell flow anticlockwise.
Compute A<sub>R</sub>, δ<sub>R</sub> for each cell and δ for every shared wall.
Write the rate of twist of each cell, (δ<sub>R</sub> q<sub>R</sub> − Σ δ<sub>RS</sub> q<sub>S</sub>)/(2A<sub>R</sub> G).
Set the rates equal: n − 1 equations for n cells.
Add the torque equation T = Σ2A<sub>R</sub> q<sub>R</sub> and solve.
Report outer walls as q<sub>R</sub> and shared walls as differences.

blocks.text: The equations are linear, so they go straight into a matrix solver: a program that sets up the coefficients and solves them is a common exercise, and the second example below is one. Walls that carry only shear (ineffective in bending) still appear in δ; only booms and walls that carry direct stress appear in I<sub>xx</sub>.

For a shear load, cut one wall in each cell to make the section open, find q<sub>b</sub> as for an open section, and add an unknown constant q<sub>s,0,R</sub> in each cell. There are then n + 1 unknowns: the n constants and the rate of twist. The equations are the n twist equations, with q<sub>b</sub> included in each integral, and one moment equation: the moments of all the flows about any point equal the moment of the applied load about that point. A constant flow q in cell R contributes 2A<sub>R</sub> q to that moment.
To find the shear centre, set the rate of twist to zero, solve the n twist equations for the constants, and the moment equation then gives the position of the load that causes no twist.

spec.aria: A long rectangle divided by a middle spar into a front cell and a longer rear cell, with six circular booms at the spar ends, larger at the front: 1200, 900 and 600 square millimetres. Upward arrows on the three spars are labelled 147.72, 100.31 and 51.97 newtons per millimetre. The skins carry 14.39 in cell 1 and 14.70 in cell 2, clockwise. A 60 kilonewton upward load arrow acts at 200 millimetres; the shear centre S is marked at 287.4 millimetres. A note gives the twist as 0.134 degrees per metre, nose up.

examples.question: A two-cell box is 200 mm deep. Cell 1 is 200 mm wide and cell 2 is 125 mm wide. The outer walls are 1.5 mm thick and the shared wall 2 mm. It carries T = 20 kN·m, with G = 27 GPa. Find the cell flows, the shared-wall flow and stress, and the rate of twist.
steps: Shared wall: q₁ − q₂ = 17.4 N/mm, τ = 17.4/2 = 8.7 N/mm². Outer walls: τ = 107.0 N/mm² in cell 1 and 95.4 N/mm² in cell 2.
examples.answer: q₁ = 160.5 N/mm, q₂ = 143.2 N/mm; the shared wall carries 17.4 N/mm (8.7 N/mm²); both cells twist at 1.749° per metre.

examples.question: A two-cell wing box, idealised into six booms that carry all the direct stress, has spars at x = 0, 300 and 800 mm and booms at y = ±100 mm: 1200 mm² on the front spar, 900 mm² on the middle spar and 600 mm² on the rear spar. The skins are 1.5 mm, the spar webs 3.0, 2.5 and 2.0 mm. A lift shear S<sub>y</sub> = 60 kN acts at x = 200 mm. With G = 27 GPa, find the cell constants q<sub>s,0,1</sub> and q<sub>s,0,2</sub>, the rate of twist, and the shear centre, using a program.
steps: Cut the top skin of each cell. Each spar web then carries only the jump at its top boom: front −133.33, middle −100.00, rear −66.67 N/mm, positive downwards; the bottom skins carry zero (the bottom boom cancels the top one).

Moments about the front spar mid-point: the spar flows give 16,666,667 N·mm, the cell constants 2A₁q<sub>s,0,1</sub> + 2A₂q<sub>s,0,2</sub> = 120,000q<sub>s,0,1</sub> + 200,000q<sub>s,0,2</sub>, and the load 60,000 × 200 = 12 × 10⁶ N·mm.
The program puts the two twist equations and the moment equation into a 3 × 3 matrix and solves them.

Final flows: front spar 147.72 N/mm, middle spar 100.31 N/mm and rear spar 51.97 N/mm, all upwards; they add to 300 N/mm × 200 mm = 60 kN, which checks. The skins carry 14.39 N/mm (cell 1) and 14.70 N/mm (cell 2), clockwise.
examples.answer: q<sub>s,0,1</sub> = −14.39 N/mm and q<sub>s,0,2</sub> = −14.70 N/mm; the box twists at 0.134° per metre (clockwise, nose up, because the lift acts ahead of the shear centre); the shear centre is 287.4 mm behind the front spar.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
# Two-cell wing box, 6 booms (x, y, B) in mm and mm^2; walls carry shear only
B = {1: (0, 100, 1200), 2: (300, 100, 900), 3: (800, 100, 600),
     4: (800, -100, 600), 5: (300, -100, 900), 6: (0, -100, 1200)}
Sy, xS, G = 60e3, 200.0, 27e3          # shear (N) acting at x = 200 mm; G in N/mm^2
Ixx = sum(b * y**2 for x, y, b in B.values())
k = Sy / Ixx
# basic flows with the top skins 1-2 and 2-3 cut; spars run downwards
qb = {(1, 6): -k * B[1][2] * B[1][1],
      (2, 5): -k * B[2][2] * B[2][1],
      (3, 4): -k * B[3][2] * B[3][1]}     # bottom skins carry zero
# walls of each cell taken anticlockwise: (from, to, length, t)
cell = {1: [(1, 6, 200, 3.0), (6, 5, 300, 1.5), (5, 2, 200, 2.5), (2, 1, 300, 1.5)],
        2: [(2, 5, 200, 2.5), (5, 4, 500, 1.5), (4, 3, 200, 2.0), (3, 2, 500, 1.5)]}
A = {1: 300 * 200, 2: 500 * 200}
def qb_dir(a, b):                       # basic flow in the direction a -> b
    return qb.get((a, b), -qb.get((b, a), 0.0))
row = []
for c in (1, 2):
    lb = sum(qb_dir(a, b) * L / t for a, b, L, t in cell[c])   # integral of qb/t
    d = sum(L / t for a, b, L, t in cell[c])
    dsh = 200 / 2.5                                             # shared mid spar
    row.append((lb, d, dsh))
# unknowns [q01, q02, rate]: twist of each cell, then moments about (0, 0)
Mqb = sum(-qb[(i, j)] * 200 * B[i][0] for i, j in qb)          # upward spar forces x arm
K = np.array([[row[0][1], -row[0][2], -2 * A[1] * G],
              [-row[1][2], row[1][1], -2 * A[2] * G],
              [2 * A[1], 2 * A[2], 0.0]])
r = np.array([-row[0][0], -row[1][0], Sy * xS - Mqb])
q01, q02, rate = np.linalg.solve(K, r)
print(f"Ixx = {Ixx:.4g} mm^4")
print(f"q01 = {q01:.2f} N/mm, q02 = {q02:.2f} N/mm")
print(f"twist rate = {rate:.3e} rad/mm = {rate * 1e3 * 180 / np.pi:.3f} deg/m")
for (i, j), v in qb.items():
    print(f"spar {i}-{j}: q = {v:.2f} N/mm before q0")
# shear centre: zero twist, solve the first two rows with rate = 0
q1s, q2s = np.linalg.solve(K[:2, :2], r[:2])
print(f"shear centre x = {(Mqb + 2 * A[1] * q1s + 2 * A[2] * q2s) / Sy:.1f} mm")

traps: Adding q₁ and q₂ in the shared wall. They oppose each other there; the wall carries q₁ − q₂.
Using the torque equation alone. Each extra cell needs an equal-twist equation.
Taking ∮ds/t over the whole outer boundary for each cell. Each integral goes round its own cell, the shared wall included.
Under shear, forgetting q<sub>b</sub> inside the twist integrals. Only for pure torque is the cell flow constant.
Calling δ a length. ∮ds/t is a length divided by a length, so it has no unit.

quiz.q: What flow does the wall shared by two cells carry?
quiz.a: The difference of the two cell flows, q₁ − q₂ in the sense of cell 1.

quiz.q: Why must the cells of a multi-cell box twist at the same rate?
quiz.a: They share walls and the ribs hold the section shape, so the whole section rotates as one. Different twist rates would tear the shared wall.

quiz.q: Equal twist gives q₂ = 0.8q₁ for a box with A₁ = 50,000 mm² and A₂ = 30,000 mm². Find the flows for T = 14.8 kN·m.
In the first example, what torque does each cell carry?
quiz.a: Cell 1: 2A₁q₁ = 12.84 kN·m; cell 2: 2A₂q₂ = 7.16 kN·m; total 20.00 kN·m.

quiz.q: How many unknowns and equations does a three-cell box under shear have?
quiz.a: Four unknowns: three cell constants and the rate of twist. Four equations: one twist equation per cell (each including q<sub>b</sub>) and one moment equation.

quiz.q: In the second example, how would you make the box carry the lift without twisting?
quiz.a: Move the load line to the shear centre, 287.4 mm behind the front spar, or move the shear centre forward by adding area or thickness at the front spar. With the load at 200 mm the offset is 87.4 mm and the box twists.

beyond: Not for the exam. A damaged-cell check assumes one cell is cracked and asks whether the rest can carry the torque. Search for "multi-cell torque box fail-safe".
